subject: physics
title: Conservation and dissipation of energy
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Conservation and dissipation of energy — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.1.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Conservation and dissipation of energy, specification section 4.1.2.
final_note: You worked through Conservation and dissipation of energy — 15 specification statements.

concepts.def: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but it cannot be created or destroyed. The total energy before a change is always equal to the total energy after it.
A system in which no energy enters or leaves. Energy can still be transferred between the stores inside a closed system, but there is no net change to the total energy of the system.
The spreading out of energy into stores that are less useful, most often the thermal store of the surroundings. Energy is dissipated in all system changes.

The everyday name for energy that has been dissipated. It has not been destroyed; it has been stored in a way that cannot be used for the intended purpose, for example in the thermal store of a warm motor.
Putting a substance such as oil between surfaces that move over each other. The friction between the surfaces is reduced, so less energy is dissipated to thermal stores as the machine runs.
A layer of material of low thermal conductivity placed around an object or a building to reduce the rate of energy transfer by conduction to the surroundings.
A property of a material, used here only as a comparison: the higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material.

concepts.term: Rate of cooling of a building
concepts.def: How quickly a building transfers energy to colder surroundings. The rate of cooling is lower when the walls are thicker and when the walls are made of a material with a lower thermal conductivity.

An investigation of the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators, and of the factors that affect the thermal insulation properties of a material, such as the thickness of the layer and the number of layers used.

concepts.term: Control variables in the insulation practical
concepts.def: The quantities kept the same so that only the material or the thickness affects the result: the volume and starting temperature of the water, the size of the container, the room temperature and the time over which the temperature is measured.

concepts.term: AT 1 and AT 5 in this practical
concepts.def: AT 1 is the use of appropriate apparatus to make and record measurements of length, temperature and time; AT 5 is making measurements of energy and temperature changes. Both are exercised by measuring the thickness of the insulating layer with a ruler and by recording the fall in water temperature at set times.

Working scientifically and mathematical skills developed in this practical: taking repeat readings for each material, identifying anomalous results, calculating a mean temperature drop and plotting the results so that materials can be compared.

The share of the energy supplied to a device that is transferred usefully. The energy efficiency for any energy transfer can be calculated using the equation: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer). Efficiency is a ratio, so it has no unit and can never be greater than 1.
Efficiency may also be calculated using the equation: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input). Both powers must be in the same unit, and the answer is again a ratio with no unit.

Making a larger share of the input energy transfer useful by reducing the unwanted transfers: lubricating moving parts, insulating hot components, streamlining a moving object to reduce air resistance and using thicker wires of lower resistance.

mcqs.q: A torch is left switched on until its battery is flat. What has happened to the energy that was in the chemical store of the battery?
options: It has been transferred to light and to thermal stores, so the total is unchanged.
It has slowly been used up, so there is less energy now than at the start.
The part of it that was wasted has been destroyed inside the torch.
It is stored in the bulb and is released again when the torch cools.
mcqs.explain: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it has been transferred usefully and dissipated, leaving the total the same.

mcqs.q: A ball bearing rolls along a bench and slowly comes to rest. The ball, the bench and the surrounding air are treated as a closed system. What is true of the total energy of this system?
options: It has fallen, because friction has let some of the energy leak out of it.
It has fallen, because energy was used up in slowing the ball down.
It is unchanged; the kinetic store has emptied into the thermal stores.
It has risen, because the friction has created extra thermal energy.
mcqs.explain: In a closed system there is no net change to the total energy; the energy has only moved between stores inside it.

mcqs.q: In every system change some of the energy is dissipated. What does dissipated mean?
options: The energy is stored in the surroundings and later returns to the system.
The energy is stored in less useful ways, usually in thermal stores.
The energy is shared out equally between all the stores in the system.
The energy is destroyed as it spreads out into the surroundings.
mcqs.explain: This is what the specification means by dissipation: energy ends up in stores that cannot do the intended job.

mcqs.q: A food mixer is running. Which energy transfer in the mixer is best described as ‘wasted’?
options: The transfer to the kinetic store of the rotating blades.
The transfer that is destroyed by friction in the bearings.
The transfer to the room that flows back into the mixer later.
The transfer to the thermal store of the warm motor.
mcqs.explain: Energy that warms the motor is dissipated: it is stored in a less useful way and cannot turn the blades.

mcqs.q: The bearings of a machine are oiled regularly. Why does this reduce the unwanted energy transfers?
options: The oil takes in the wasted energy and stores it so it can be used again.
There is less friction, so less energy is dissipated to the thermal stores.
The oil removes the friction entirely, so no energy is dissipated.
The oil makes the moving parts lighter and so easier to turn.
mcqs.explain: Lubrication lowers the friction between the moving surfaces, so a smaller share of the input is dissipated.

mcqs.q: Thick insulation is laid in the loft of a house. Which statement about the house is now correct?
options: No energy can leave through the loft now, so the house never cools.
The insulation gives out warmth of its own and heats the rooms up.
The building now cools down more slowly than it did before.
The energy is destroyed inside the insulating material.
mcqs.explain: The insulation lowers the rate of energy transfer through the loft, so the building cools more slowly.

mcqs.q: Two saucepan handles are the same size and shape, but one is made from a material with a higher thermal conductivity than the other. Which statement about that handle is correct?
options: It transfers energy by conduction at a higher rate than the other one.
It transfers energy more slowly, because it holds the energy inside itself.
It transfers energy at the same rate, as the handles match in size.
It must be thicker in order to conduct energy at that rate.
mcqs.explain: The higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across it.

mcqs.q: Two houses are identical except that one has thicker outside walls, built from the same brick. On a cold night, compared with the other house, the house with the thicker walls will
options: cool down faster, because there is more brick that has to be warmed up.
cool at the same rate, because the brick has the same conductivity.
warm itself up, because the thick walls give energy to the rooms.
cool down more slowly than the house with thinner walls.
mcqs.explain: For the same material, a thicker wall gives a lower rate of energy transfer, so the building cools more slowly.

mcqs.q: An architect wants a new building to cool down as slowly as possible on a cold night. Which change should be made to its walls?
options: Build them from a material that has a higher thermal conductivity.
Make them thinner so that less brick has to be warmed up first.
Make them thicker and use a material of lower thermal conductivity.
Keep the thickness but choose a brick that conducts more quickly.
mcqs.explain: Both factors act the same way: greater thickness and lower thermal conductivity each lower the rate of cooling.

mcqs.q: In required practical activity 2, identical beakers of hot water are wrapped in different materials and the water temperature is recorded for ten minutes. Which result identifies the best insulator?
options: The beaker whose water fell in temperature by the smallest amount.
The beaker whose water fell in temperature by the largest amount of all.
The beaker whose water was the hottest when the timing started.
The beaker whose water ended at the temperature of the room.
mcqs.explain: The best insulator gives the lowest rate of energy transfer, so its water stays hottest and drops least.

mcqs.q: A student investigates how the thickness of an insulating layer affects the cooling of hot water in a beaker. Which measurements should be taken?
options: The temperature of the water at the end of the run, and nothing else.
The temperature of the room, measured at the start and again at the end.
The thickness of the layer, and the water temperature at set times.
The mass of the insulation and the volume of the water used.
mcqs.explain: AT 1 and AT 5 are exercised here: the length is measured with a ruler and the temperature is recorded against time.

mcqs.q: The student repeats the cooling run three times for each material and calculates a mean temperature drop. Why is this done?
options: So that the water is given more time in which to cool down properly.
To reduce the effect of random error and give a more reliable result.
To make every material finish at the same final temperature.
To change the independent variable several times over.
mcqs.explain: Repeat readings scatter because of random variation; a mean of several runs is more reliable and reveals anomalies.

mcqs.q: A small electric motor is supplied with 800 J of energy. Of this, 260 J is transferred usefully to a kinetic store. What is the efficiency of the motor?
mcqs.explain: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer) = 260 J / 800 J = 0.325.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the efficiency of a device is correct?
options: A very well made device can have an efficiency of more than 1.
The efficiency of a device can never be greater than 1.
Efficiency is measured in joules when energy values are used.
Efficiency gives the fraction of the input energy wasted.
mcqs.explain: The useful output energy transfer cannot exceed the total input energy transfer, so the ratio is at most 1.

mcqs.q: A motor has a total power input of 1200 W and a useful power output of 900 W. What is the efficiency of the motor?
mcqs.explain: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input) = 900 W / 1200 W = 0.75, a ratio with no unit.

mcqs.q: (HT) A gearbox wastes energy because of friction between its moving parts. Which change would increase the efficiency of the intended energy transfer?
options: Lubricate the moving parts to reduce the energy dissipated.
Supply more power to the gearbox, so that it does more work each second.
Remove the friction completely so the gearbox is 100% efficient.
Run the gearbox for less time, so that less energy is wasted overall.
mcqs.explain: Reducing an unwanted transfer leaves a larger share of the input as useful output, which raises the efficiency.
